<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but A pressed a structural critique that B never fully resolved: when forced to define the trigger precisely, B named "any denial, cut, or termination of benefits, any deportation... any decision lengthening criminal exposure" — which A correctly identified as swallowing nearly the entire caseload of these agencies, contradicting B's earlier claim that the right was narrow and workable. B's closing response ("of course it does — the caseload is lives") is rhetorically strong but does not answer the feasibility problem A raised consistently: either the right applies everywhere and collapses processing speed, or agencies triage cases and the automated "gate" problem B claims to solve reopens. A also landed a sharp, mostly unanswered rebuttal in Rebuttal 2: B's own fix for the rubber-stamp problem (individualized reasons, engagement with evidence, documented departures, liability) is a procedural test that does not inherently require a human body — meaning B's remedy converges on A's proposed alternative (audits, explanation duties, targeted appeal) rather than refuting it. B's normative core — that coercive state power requires a named, accountable human — remained compelling and was never fully dismantled, and B's flip on delay (automated wrongful denials also cause destitution) was a good counter that A did not fully re-engage after Rebuttal 1. But by the closing, A had the cleaner, more resolved path: B's own concessions under pressure did more damage to B's case than B's answers did to repair it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 point that B's procedural fix for rubber-stamping (individualized reasons, record engagement, documented departures, liability) does not require a human decision-maker and is functionally identical to A's own proposed remedy — a concession B's closing never adequately answered.</best_rebuttal>
